author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In Tk̓emlúps, community gathers to ‘reclaim our space’ and denounce white nationalism
content:
At the same site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc on Sunday, more than 100 Secwépemc people and their allies returned to the area two days later to reclaim the space. They drummed, sang and prayed to cleanse the spot, which is located a few hundred metres away from the former Kamloops Indian Residential School. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Content warning: This article contains details about residential “schools.” Please read with care for your spirit.







On the eve of Orange Shirt Day, more than 100 people gathered in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc to cleanse and reclaim a site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred earlier this week.




For nearly three hours on Tuesday night, Secwépemc people and their allies drummed, sang and prayed — for the land and the people, and for all the families impacted by residential “schools.”




Secwépemc people and their allies drum, sing and pray on Tuesday, near the site where a white nationalist demonstration took place in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc two days prior. 

Photo by Aaron Hemens




Ashley Michel from Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc organized Tuesday’s gathering with four other Secwépemc (Shuswap) mothers.

author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: New book aims to ‘push back and defend survivors’ against denialism
content:
Pre-signed copies of ‘Truth Before Reconciliation’ were made available for audience goers of the September 17 launch in Winnipeg. Photo by Crystal Greene




Outside a Winnipeg bookstore, about 25 volunteers in orange shirts formed a welcoming line as sage smoke rose from an abalone shell. 




Inside McNally Robinson Booksellers, more than 300 people gathered for the launch of 

Truth Before Reconciliation: Confronting Residential School Denialism

. Outside, the volunteers helped provide security as organizers anticipated denialists might try to disrupt the event on September 17. 




“We want to make sure that it’s safe for the survivors,” said Emma Tardiff, one of the volunteers. “I really care about my community.”




Published by University of Manitoba Press ahead of National Day for Truth and Reconciliation, the collection grew from an effort by scholars and authors to confront the denial and downplaying of what survivors experienced. 




The book consists of 13 chapters that include survivor interviews, expert analysis and examination of the denialism movement. Contributors include historians, educators, survivors, archivists and archaeologists, alongside the book’s two co-editors, Sean Carlton and Niigaan Sinclair.

author: Dionne Phillips, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Indigenous New York Fashion Week brings family and futurity to the runway
content:
Details at Cheyenne LeGrande’s show at Indigenous NYFW on Sept. 11. Photo by Dionne Philips




Backstage at Indigenous New York Fashion Week (INYFW), Dusty LeGrande helped lace up garments from his sibling Cheyenne Rain LeGrande’s collection. A year earlier, Cheyenne had been there to model and help him with his own designs.




“It’s kind of so special because now he’s backstage with me, helping me lace up these garments, and it’s kind of nice that we can help each other out in that way,” she told IndigiNews.




The artist from Bigstone Cree Nation closed the Emerging Voices show on Sept. 11 with a collection that included laced-up mini skirts, tops with jingle dress cones and a wearable art piece made from 3,300 pop can tabs and ribbons.




A model showcasing LeGrande’s designs including the piece made from pop tabs and ribbons. Photo by Dionne Phillips




INYFW’s second year ran from Sept. 10 to 15, bringing together 30 Indigenous designers for six shows in Lenapehoking (Lenape homelands), on the island Mannahatta (Manhattan).




Just off Fashion Avenue, the American Indian Community House was transformed for the event, with seats lining the runway and fabric cascading to the floor.




Korina Emmerich (Puyallup descent) and Liana Shewey (Mvskoke), co-founders of Relative Arts and INYFW, organized the event with volunteers and professionals.

author: Frey Blake-Pijogge, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In a changing northern landscape, Inuit bear guards keep people safe in the wilderness
content:
A nanuk (polar bear) in Tongait KakKasuangita SilakKijapvinga (Torngat Mountains National Park) in northern ‘Labrador.’ 

Photo by Frey Blake-Pijogge




After retiring from his career as a federal conservation officer, Derrick Pottle — an Inuk Elder from Tikigâksuagusik (Rigolet) — devoted himself to guiding people on the land, carving, hunting, and training bear guards.




The seasoned instructor and guide founded BearSafe Planning in 2005, which trains and certifies students to perform the role of guarding for the bear species found in the region and beyond — including polar bears, grizzly bears and black bears. 




Pottle’s three-day course is advertised as offering “safety, protection, confidence in bear country.” Bear guards work to monitor for bears  and prevent encounters with humans out on the land.




“The whole objective of the course,” he told IndigiNews, is firstly “people’s safety” around bears. But that aim “is followed very closely” by “bear safety,” he explained.




“We want to prepare people … to recognize some of the potential signs that the bear is not comfortable,” he continued. “They may feel threatened, they may feel intimidated, and they may even charge or attack you.”




He teaches his students “how to recognize those signs, how to prepare yourself for them, the tools you have to use to do your job.”

author: Santana Dreaver
title: After more than a century, this Salish woolly dog pelt has returned to ‘B.C.’
content:
Only known pelt of the extinct woolly dog. Photo by Brittany M. Hance, courtesy of Division of Mammals, Smithsonian

Institution 




This story is co-published 

with the Narwhal

 as part of their 

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship







Coming face to face with the pelt of a now-extinct Salish woolly dog was an emotional experience for Jordan Wilson.




The curator from xʷməθkʷəy̓əm (Musqueam Indian Band) attended an unveiling at the Museum of Anthropology in “Vancouver” as the ancestor was welcomed back to its home territories earlier this month.




The pelt is on loan from the Smithsonian institution, where it was in storage for more than a century — it was sent to the “American” museum in 1859. It will be at MOA until August of 2027. 




Belonging to a dog from Stó:lō territories known as Mutton, it’s the only known Salish woolly dog pelt in existence.




As the pelt was unveiled to its Salish relatives on Sept. 4, Wilson attended along with other Salish community members from “Vancouver Island” and the “Fraser Valley.”




“For me personally, I was caught off guard at the emotional quality of it,” Wilson said.




“Seeing this pelt in person, seeing its little paws and seeing its little nose, realizing that this was a living being that was alive 160 years ago.”

author: Crystal Greene, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Indigenous volunteers are helping care for ‘rez dog’ relatives — with little funding
content:
June Thomas, with Ginew Animal Care Services on Roseau River Anishinabe First Nation, holds a puppy on her reserve in southern Manitoba. 

Photo courtesy Ginew Animal Care Services/Facebook




As an animal lover, June Thomas grew increasingly concerned about the many stray dogs and cats roaming her community’s reserve in southern Manitoba — and decided to do something about them. 




What started as a home operation to better care for the animals in 2017, which she called “June’s Adoptables,” has since grown into a full animal shelter on Roseau River Anishinabe First Nation (RRAFN), nearly 100 kilometres south of Winnipeg. 




Thomas believes the shelter, which opened in February, is the first one on-reserve in the province.




“I started off in my own house rescuing animals like dogs and cats,” Thomas told IndigiNews. 




She was inspired to take action after her beloved dog Bessie became sick and died from canine parvovirus, a highly contagious 

disease

 commonly known as parvo. 




Eventually, June’s Adoptables outgrew Thomas’s house — and she became incorporated as 

Ginew Animal Care Services

.




“I took a veterinary assistant program,” said Thomas, who graduated in 2024 from Robertson College and is now certified to give vaccinations. 




“It gave me the skills and helped me want to set up a shelter.”




On reserves, “rez dogs” are beloved mixed-breed strays

author: Dionne Phillips, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: Docuseries features action-packed Snuneymuxw canoe club: ‘Our culture is alive and well’
content:
A still from ‘Racing Waters’ shows the Island Brave Canoe Club on the water fighting for the lead. Submitted image




A new docuseries showcases the fast-paced sport of canoe racing — with sprawling overhead views of competitions to close-up shots of rapid-fire paddles on the water.




Over nine episodes, 

Racing Waters

 follows Snuneymuxw First Nation’s Island Brave Canoe Club located on “Vancouver Island.”




There are multiple competitions included in the series  — including single, double and six person races — but the 11-man war canoe races remain the main event. 




“Eleven-man is the main show, and everybody comes out to watch that,“ said Eli Wyse, a paddler on the Island Brave team and a member of Snuneymuxw First Nation.




Beyond the large in-person crowds that races draw on the West Coast and beyond, 

Racing Waters

 brings that spirit to audiences across the country, with a high energy and connection to the sport that can be felt through the screen. The in-depth portrayal of the sport includes highlighting the culture and humanity attached to it. 




The docuseries premiered on Sept. 13 on APTN. It’s already been renewed and filming is underway for season two.

The Island Brave team carries their canoe. Submitted image

author: Santana Dreaver
title: Call in the goats: Kanaka Bar recruits herd for help with wildfire risk
content:
Wildfire fighting goats are pictured in Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens




This article has been co-published 

with the Narwhal

 as part of their 

2026 Indigenous journalism fellowship







On a grassy slope in Kanaka Bar, a herd of goats frolic and play. But this isn’t a farm or a petting zoo — it’s an innovative wildfire mitigation effort from the First Nation.




Some of the goats loudly bleat as they chow down on invasive species and overgrown brush. 




A wildfire fighting goat eats vegetation in Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Photo by Aaron Hemens




“In the last five years, Kanaka community has been experiencing devastation with fire,” Pauline Michell said.




That includes two evacuations due to wildfires, as well as floods and mudslides that have closed roads and 

cut off

 her community from the world. And in Kanaka Bar, there is no fire truck or fire hall. 




“Kanaka has solely been on its own in regards to fire,” said Michell. 




Located in Nlaka’pamux territory, twenty kilometers south of Lytton, Kanaka Bar Indian Band also goes by T’eqt’ aqtn’mux, “the crossing place people.” 




A helper greets one of the wildfire fighting goats in Kanaka Bar, B.C., on Sept. 1, 2026. Aaron Hemens/The Narwhal
